units.translation: μέλαν δρυός [the black of the oak] is the black of the oak, i.e. the heartwood of the oak, as in Homer Od. 14, 12 σταυροὺς δ᾽ ἐκτὸς ἔλασσε – πυκνοὺς καὶ θαμέας , τὸ μέλαν δρυός ἀμφικεάσσας [he drove stakes outside, close and thick, splitting off the black of the oak]. Hence the adjective μελάνδρυος [of the black of the oak] is formed, about which the scholiast says: "τὸ μέλαν δρυὸς τὴν ἑντεριώνην φασὶν οὕτω καλου-μένην [they say the black of the oak is the heartwood, so called]; Aristarchus says it is the bark; Crates says it is the thickness of the leaves (thus I corrected from Eustathius for τὴν τῶν δασυτάτων φυτῶν [the thickest of plants]) μέλαν δρυός [the black of the oak], as Aeschylus also says in Philoctetes (fr. 249) "κρεμάσασα τόξον [having hung the bow] (κρεμάσας τόξον [having hung the bow] Eustathius, κρεμαστὰ τόξα [hung bows] Hermann) πίτυος ἐκ μελαν-δρύου [from the black of the pine]. But δρυὸς [of the oak] can also be understood of any wood."

Improperly Suppl. 530 λίμνᾳ δ᾽ ἔμβαλε πορφυροειδεῖ τὰν μελανόζυγ᾽ ἄταν [and cast into the purple lake the black-benched ruin].

στέρφεσιν αἰγείοις [with goat skins]: τοῖς δέρμασιν [with the hides]; hence also στερφῶσαι [to cover with hides]. Ibicus called the army στερφωτῆρα στρατὸν [hide-clad army], meaning the one having hides. Hence also in Aeschylus (fr. 389) they think it right to write "με-λανοστέρφων [of the black-skinned] (thus the copies: μελαστέρφων L. μελανστέρφων Nauck) γένος [race], not, as some, μελανοστέρνων [of the black-chested]; for they have not only their chests black, but also their whole body; hence also the jar is called στέρφος [hide].
O black and perfect curse of the race of Oedipus
